excerpt_original: With La Dolce Vista, Claude Nori returns to his contact sheets and draws from them black-and-white images, most of them unpublished, from Italy and beyond. A book of love memories by the man who founded Contrejour in 1975 and quietly reshaped the landscape of French photography.…

blocks.text: One letter, and everything shifts. Dolce Vita , Dolce Vista : the sweetness of living becomes the sweetness of seeing. Claude Nori has never hidden his debt to Federico Fellini, and here he settles it in full, from the very first page. The film’s final shot, then. The beach at Fregene, at dawn. Marcello, tipsy in his white suit, kneeling in the sand after one last night of debauchery. Across a tiny inlet, Paola, the young waitress from the trattoria, calls out to him and improvises a graceful little dance. The wind drowns out her voice. Marcello shrugs, gives up, and goes back to his friends. Paola smiles at the camera. The end. “This black-and-white image, the portrait of a young girl in a dress in a seaside landscape of southern Italy, seeming to wait for a sign from destiny, was the origin of my photographic work,” he says. Ever since, Paola has slipped into his framing “like an inner music.” And Claude Nori wonders whether he has spent his life trying to erase the regret of watching Marcello turn his back on beauty. He himself never does.

blocks.caption: Isabelle , Nice, 1997 © Claude Nori

blocks.text: Born in 1949 in Toulouse to Italian parents, who opened the city’s first Italian restaurant there (every Italian in the area came to eat), Claude Nori spent his summers on the Adriatic coast, in Rimini especially. He wanted to make films, took classes in Toulouse and then in Paris, but discovered photography in 1968. Cinema has remained an undercurrent. “What I love is telling stories. Every photo is a story.” There was also Agnès Varda, his neighbor in Paris’s 14th arrondissement, who opened doors for him. How did he meet her? “At first, it was my butcher who told me she lived across the street from me.” You couldn’t make it up. One day, he even came across Catherine Deneuve and Marcello Mastroianni in the courtyard—the Marcello of La Dolce Vita himself.

But the source goes further back, and it is his mother’s. “My mother’s world was idyllic. With her everything was pretty, the flowers, the songs, the memories of love, a continuous photo-novel,” reads the opening of the book. On the phone from Biarritz, Claude Nori explains: his mother cried when she told him about her childhood, her love for a fairground man with a lovely voice, the operas in Verona, Madame Butterfly , La Bohème . “It was very romantic, very corny even, but I liked it.” At home there were piles of photo-novels, then in their golden age in Italy: almost every film had its own. “It was wonderful, because it was a set of still photographs that told a story.” Still photographs telling a story: that is precisely what Chris Marker does with La Jetée (1962), which he subtitled a “photo-novel.” A lasting memory. “I said to myself, ‘That’s it, that’s really what can be done.’” Claude did try his hand at Super 8, shooting a film on the beaches of Rimini that he sold to television. “I don’t care about synchronized sound,” he told himself at the time. “What I want is to capture things.” But in the end the book won out, with that “kind of kinetics produced by turning the pages.” François Truffaut’s Stolen Kisses is never far away.

blocks.text: Who remembers that in the mid-1970s, photography in France had almost nowhere to be shown? Claude Nori does. “There was no internet, so we created the internet in Arles,” he sums up. He arrived there in 1975, among what he calls a “tribe”: people shouted in the amphitheater when they had to, put the world to rights on the Place du Forum, and talked about printing, since every photographer developed their own images back then. Then the Americans arrived, Ralph Gibson and Ansel Adams among them, and the festival grew. That same year, in July, he presented the first issue of Contrejour in the courtyard of the Hôtel L’Arlatan, a magazine whose layouts were inspired by Anglo-Saxon fanzines and whose cover showed the photographer Roger Vulliez slashing his stomach with a dagger (no less). Hervé Guibert reviewed it in Le Monde . In 1976, Claude Nori became his own publisher and released his first book, Lunettes (Glasses).

Over the next twenty years came some one hundred and sixty titles , including first books that mattered: Bernard Plossu and Le Voyage mexicain (The Mexican Journey), Guy Le Querrec, Martine Franck, Jean Gaumy, Jeanloup Sieff, Sebastião Salgado, Pierre et Gilles. Elders too: Édouard Boubat, Willy Ronis, Sabine Weiss. In 1978 he published La Photographie française des origines à nos jours (French Photography from Its Origins to the Present Day), written at breakneck speed: he met some twenty photographers in Paris, who sent him on to others. Lartigue, Brassaï, Cartier-Bresson. “They liked it when a young man came to see them and said, ‘Well, I really like what you do, and by the way, would you know another photographer?’” In 1981 came Les Cahiers de la photographie , with Gilles Mora and Jean-Claude Lemagny, a journal of criticism modeled on Les Cahiers du cinéma . In 1983, again with Gilles Mora, L’Été dernier, Manifeste photobiographique (Last Summer, a Photobiographical Manifesto) laid the foundations of a first-person photography, somewhere between reportage and fiction. A pioneer? Yes, and without making a fuss about it. Contrejour closed in 1995 and was reborn in 2011 with Isabelle, his wife, in Biarritz, where he has lived since 1999 and where he founded the Terre d’Images festival.

blocks.text: His friends? Jeanloup Sieff, Bernard Plossu, Franco Fontana and Luigi Ghirri. A beach scene: Ghirri, sweating, with his tripod and his heavy 6×7, taking forever to set up; Nori beside him with a little plastic camera. “I had my little thing, click, click, click,” he says with amusement. They drove together listening to Bob Dylan, whose concerts Ghirri never missed. “Someone lively, funny, amused by the world.” When he tells this to Italian critics, they are astonished. And then there was Édouard Boubat, who would call him for a walk in the Luxembourg Gardens. A few photos, a cup of tea, a pretty girl walking by. “Did you see how beautiful she is?” Yes.

Because that is the real subject. “Romantic love, with its liveliness and its torments, has been the main subject of my books,” writes Claude Nori, who has signed about fifteen under his own name. For this one, Isabelle pushed him to reopen his negatives. “There are lots of beautiful photos I had overlooked,” he admits. The films had been properly loaded, following a craftsman’s rule he recalls at the end of the book: make sure the film “will defy time.” The result: 172 pages of black and white, from 1973 to 2015, with Italy at the center, but also Paris, Nice, Seville, Veracruz and the Dune du Pilat. A gate in the mist of the Po Valley (1991). A man leaping, umbrella in the air, on the shore of Lake Garda (1995). A young woman on a scooter outside the Zanichelli publishing house in Bologna (1996). A black dog in front of a merry-go-round. Rimini, again and always, and a summer that never ends, since, as he writes, “winter is a film that covers summer.” And the grain of Tri-X, “an almost carnal texture.” His favorite images? The most anonymous ones. “It’s like in a film: an anonymous place, all it takes is one thing well placed, an atmosphere.”

blocks.text: Between the photographs, Claude Nori has slipped in texts taken from his youthful notebooks, the ones he filled “when I was in love, sad or elated, which is to say often.” None of it is invented, he insists: these are real people. First there is Adèle, his childhood friend and accomplice. He met her in Rome one morning as she let down her hair and ordered a Campari, and it was in her company that he wrote: “I truly feel Italian.” There is also the girl at the bumper cars. He watched her for a long time from the edge of the rink, a Gauloise between his lips, then set off after her at the wheel of a little car. The chase ended in a head-on collision, and she later confessed that, for her, it had been their first kiss. And there is the architecture student who rang his doorbell one day, set a magic lantern on his table and corrected him mischievously: “No, it’s a photographer’s house.”

Further on, the night of a wedding in the Corbières stretches across a page. A flowered dress slipped off bare shoulders, a bottle of bad champagne was emptied in the damp grass, and the boy was fifteen at the start of the text, then sixteen, then seventeen. From those years, Claude Nori has drawn a small philosophy: a successful evening, he notes elsewhere, is not the one of the first kiss but the one “when you understood it would be for tomorrow.” Then there is the Vespa scene, the longest in the book. Caterina and Lorenzo, sitting face to face on the narrow seat, laughed and told each other stories. The photographer approached with measured steps, like a dancer, and pressed the shutter once, twice. Lorenzo eventually called out to him, then asked him to pose with Caterina, as a souvenir. Claude Nori handed him his camera and, instead of being over the moon, suddenly feared the boy might run off with it. It could have been a scene from Dino Risi. What he is looking for in life, he has written in the margin of an image: “the rare bird.”

blocks.text: Could he make these images today? Caterina had already pointed out: “You could have asked for our permission.” Claude Nori’s answer is blunt. “No, I could never have taken the same pictures,” he says. “Today there is real mistrust; people immediately ask, ‘What is it for?’” Was the young man shy? A little, and he readily admits it. “I was shy, but since I wanted to talk to girls and photograph them, I forced myself,” he recalls. To make the encounters easier, he promised prints and tried to keep his word. He has remained friends with five or six of his subjects. His daughter, now 30, looks at these photographs from another time with astonishment. That is also why this book matters: Claude Nori built it while taking into account the way his wife and daughter see things, and he counts it among his two or three favorites. He has often been called a dilettante. “I don’t reject that,” he replies. He swims every day in Biarritz, even in big waves, and finds his dolce vista every morning with Isabelle, “savoring a vero caffè.”
La Dolce Vista , by Claude Nori, is published by Contrejour and available for €45.
